items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 9
items.excerpt: 09 November 2026• Update: 09 November 2026 Here’s a rundown of all the news you need to start your Monday, including US President Donald Trump saying he was not seeking further escalation with Iran following midterm elections, Israeli president tasking Eisenkot with forming new government, and COP31 climate summit opening in Türkiye's Antalya. US President Donald Trump said he was not seeking further escalation with Iran following the midterm elections. "I'm not looking to. I don't think there's any reason to," he said in an interview with CBS News' 60 Minutes. He also repeated his claim that Israel would not exist without US military strikes against Iran's nuclear facilities. Trump claimed the US had won the war and that Tehran was interested in reaching an agreement. "We would have had a deal except for this election," he said, suggesting the Democratic victory had complicated negotiations. Trump said a "great dislike" for Israel, public opposition to the war with Iran and rising gasoline prices were the primary reasons Republicans suffered sweeping losses in last week's midterm elections. - Israeli president tasks Eisenkot with forming new government Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Sunday tasked Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new government after parliamentary elections left his bloc and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s alliance short of a majority. Eisenkot has 28 days to form a government under Israel’s Basic Law. Herzog can grant him up to 14 additional days if needed, according to the daily Yedioth Ahronoth. Herzog announced his decision to ask Eisenkot to form the next government on Saturday after consulting parliamentary factions. ​​​​​​​His office said factions representing 67 members of the 120-seat Knesset recommended Eisenkot, while factions representing 46 backed Netanyahu. A seven-member faction declined to recommend a candidate. - COP31 climate summit to open in Türkiye's Antalya The 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change will begin Monday in Türkiye's Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, bringing together heads of state, senior officials, academics, and civil society representatives from around the world. First held in Berlin in 1995, the annual summit provides a platform for countries party to the convention to assess progress in combating climate change, develop common solutions, and make decisions shaping global climate policies. Türkiye will preside over this year's conference, which runs on Nov. 9-20 and addresses key decisions on sustainable development and climate policies.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot confirmed France would attend, although its representative has not been named. Russia is sending a senior delegation including deputy foreign ministers, military officials and intelligence chiefs. Moscow has not indicated any change in its negotiating position. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that a broader US proposal could be dangerous for Ukraine, saying discussions on ending the war and security guarantees should come first. Russia launched another major attack on Kyiv ahead of the talks. US President Donald Trump said he believed the war would end soon and suggested Ukraine’s borders could change. More than 600,000 were affected in Dnipropetrovsk, with another 250,000 losing power in Kharkiv. The strikes followed earlier Russian attacks on energy facilities across the country. Repair crews are working to restore supplies but repeated attacks are complicating their efforts. Dnipropetrovsk Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said hospitals and critical infrastructure were relying on generators. The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant also lost external electricity, forcing it to use emergency diesel generators for reactor cooling and other essential safety functions. ... The records, obtained by hacking groups, include death certificates explicitly linked to the conflict. A broader calculation by one group puts the toll at approximately 450,000, including deaths not directly attributed to combat. The figures cannot be independently authenticated in full, although comparisons with previously published statistics and other casualty estimates support their credibility. Russia has not publicly disclosed military losses since the invasion’s early months, and delayed registrations mean the latest figures likely understate the toll. The data also shows unequal effects across Russian society. War-related deaths account for a substantially greater share of fatalities among younger men and residents of remote regions than among those in Moscow and St Petersburg. The findings emerge ahead of planned US-brokered ceasefire discussions in Abu Dhabi. ... Production at Iraq’s Khor Mor gas field was suspended on Sunday after an explosive-laden drone struck a liquefied petroleum gas storage tank, triggering a fire. The facility, operated by UAE-based Dana Gas in the Kurdistan region, supplies gas to most of the region’s power stations. Employees were evacuated to shelters, while Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said initial assessments indicated no casualties. ... The attack halted gas supplies and removed approximately 2.8 gigawatts of regional electricity generation capacity. Kurdish authorities said they were working to minimise disruption to the power grid. No group immediately claimed responsibility. Khor Mor has faced repeated attacks, with production previously suspended in July over security threats. ... items.title: US CPI, Fed rhetoric and Iran talks in focus after Democratic midterm sweep
items.excerpt: This week starting from November 9 places inflation back at the centre of the macro outlook. October CPI is scheduled for Tuesday, followed by PPI on Friday, while several Federal Reserve officials are due to speak during the week. Kaynat Chainwala November 09, 2026 / 07:23 IST ... A Democratic sweep of the US midterms reshaped the macro narrative this week starting from November 9, triggering a sharp unwinding in AI and technology equities and a steep repricing of oil on hopes of an Iran settlement, even as a robust jobs report kept the Federal Reserve on a higher for longer path. The dollar index initially fell to a one-month low of 101.09 as a divided government reduced expectations of fresh fiscal expansion. However, the currency reversed course after a stronger-than-expected October employment report, rising to a weekly high of 102.4 and finishing near 102.3. Payrolls increased by 1,65,000, compared with expectations of around 65,000, while unemployment declined to 4.1 percent. Wage growth of 0.4 percent month-on-month and 3.1 percent year-on-year also exceeded forecasts. Together with upward revisions totalling 84,000 jobs for August and September, the data suggested that the summer slowdown was less pronounced than previously feared. Weekly jobless claims also declined, reinforcing signs of labour-market resilience. CME data show roughly a 75 percent probability of a December hike, with Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin favouring modest increases to contain elevated inflation. The 10-year Treasury yield rose to about 4.90 percent on Friday but remained lower on the week. US equities recorded their steepest single-day decline as investors assessed whether Democratic control of Congress could result in greater regulatory scrutiny, potentially slowing AI infrastructure and data-centre development.

items.title: Jeffries backs Hegseth impeachment as Democrats vow probes of Trump allies | Donald Trump News | Al Jazeera
items.excerpt: United States House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has thrown his support behind impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, as the Democratic Party prepares to use its incoming congressional majorities to probe President Donald Trump’s administration. In a Sunday appearance on the Television show This Week with George Stephanopoulos, Jeffries weighed in on the upcoming impeachment resolution, anticipated for the coming days. “I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of defence has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran.” The impeachment resolution has been spearheaded by outgoing Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a vocal critic of the US-Israel war on Iran. “Pete Hegseth has got to go,” Jeffries added. “I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution.” ## Investigating ‘unprecedented corruption’ Jeffries is poised to become the next speaker in the House of Representatives after Democrats notched a historic victory in the November 3 midterm elections. Both the House and the Senate flipped into Democratic control, with the left-wing party making some of its biggest gains in the lower chamber in more than half a century. Democrats are expected to use their new congressional majorities to launch investigations into the Trump administration. There have also been concerns, voiced by Trump himself, that he and other top officials could face impeachment. In Sunday’s interview, Jeffries said the Democratic majority would move “aggressively” in its first 100 days in office, both to address affordability and “unprecedented corruption” under Trump. “We are committed to cleaning up the mess wherever it’s found,” Jeffries said. “That’s in Congress, in the Supreme Court, and with respect to this administration.” Currently, Republicans hold a government “trifecta”, with control of both chambers of Congress and the presidency. The Supreme Court also boasts a conservative supermajority, shaped by three Trump appointees. But a new Congress will be sworn in on January 3. In the coming weeks, Democrats will choose their party leaders for both chambers. Representative Robert Garcia formally announced his bid to lead the House Oversight Committee in a letter to colleagues on Thursday. The committee is the chamber’s principal investigative panel, with the power to subpoena witnesses and documents. ## ‘Very serious’ allegations On Sunday, Garcia told CNN that Stephen Miller‘s influential role in the Trump administration warranted investigation. Miller, who was named last week as White House chief of staff, has been closely associated with Trump’s hardline immigration policies since his first term as president. “What we think is that Stephen Miller is the architect of this horrific, unjust policy happening across the country,” Garcia said, pointing to policies of separating immigrant families and accusations of due process abuses. “Stephen Miller is at the centre of major policy decisions that are happening in the administration, and it does deserve oversight and investigation.” Garcia also signalled interest in questioning businessman Elon Musk over his leadership in the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), a federal initiative that led to widespread federal workforce cuts at the start of Trump’s second term. DOGE also sought access to sensitive government data, including Americans’ personal information. “What happened with DOGE, in particular, and the federal employees losing jobs the way they did and people’s data likely being compromised, I think, is very serious,” Garcia said. Congressional committees have the power to hold hearings, subpoena witnesses, and demand documents, giving lawmakers a constitutional check on the executive branch. The House can also impeach administration officials if a simple majority votes in favour. Conviction and removal, however, require a two-thirds vote in the Senate, a high bar even with Democrats controlling the chamber. ## Trump’s camp bites back The White House was quick to draw its own battle lines. Speaking on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said there could be investigations into Democratic lawmakers over their “threatening” rhetoric. He added he was ready to counter Democratic efforts to probe and impeach Trump officials. “If that’s what this new incoming leadership wants to do, we are ready,” said Blanche, a former personal lawyer for Trump. “If you work in this administration, you have a lawyer. It’s me.” Trump, meanwhile, made similar remarks in a Truth Social post on Saturday. He called on the Justice Department to investigate Democrats over their plans to haul his allies before congressional committees, branding them as “SLEAZEBAGS” who “should go to jail”. “The threats being made by the Democrat Party against innocent Republican Donors and Party Members are absolutely unprecedented, and totally illegal,” the president wrote.

items.title: Reuters US Domestic News Summary | International
items.excerpt: With Stephen Miller at the helm, Trump charts a course for conflict President Donald Trump's decision to elevate loyalist Stephen Miller to run his White House indicates that he plans to ramp up ​confrontation in his final two years in office and block outside political and economic pressures, Trump administration officials and other Republicans say. Voters delivered a historic rebuke to ​Republicans in Tuesday's midterm election, but with Miller as White House chief of staff, the Trump administration is expected ‌to continue ​its aggressive immigration crackdown, amplify cultural conflicts and give no ground to a Democratic-controlled Congress, say officials and experts who spoke to Reuters. They say wavering Republicans will face increased pressure to stay in line, while businesses may have a harder time making their case to the White House. Democratic wins in state AG races give Trump a new headache Democrats flipped attorney general offices in five Republican-leaning states in the midterm elections, dealing a significant blow to the conservative legal movement and erecting a new line of resistance against President Donald ‌Trump's agenda. The victories in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Iowa and Kansas threaten to disrupt conservative legal strategy. Incoming Democratic attorneys general could halt cooperation with federal immigration operations, fortify abortion access and file multistate challenges against the Trump administration's environmental and gun policies. ... Republicans lost state attorney general races to Democrats in key states in the November 3 midterm elections, with potential consequences for lawsuits related to abortion, transgender rights and other issues that the outgoing Republicans championed. Democrats will take over state attorney general offices in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and Texas. ... US anti-trans ballot wins pose challenge for Democrats ahead of 2028 Voters in four ‌US states approved ballot measures to restrict transgender rights in Tuesday's midterm elections, sending a warning to Democrats on an issue that has divided the party and is likely to remain a political challenge heading into the 2028 presidential race. The measures succeeded even as Democrats swept to victory nationwide and retook control of Congress, suggesting voters who backed Democratic candidates were still receptive to some Republican arguments on transgender issues.

items.title: Try and Stop Us Digest — November 9, 2026 — Try and Stop Us
items.excerpt: Democratic and Republican lawyers have descended on all 82 Mississippi counties as officials count the last ballots in a Senate race that Democrat Scott Colom now leads by 2,574 votes. The Guardian: Both sides are trading sharp legal letters about counting procedures. The NRSC demanded that counties separate and preserve all affidavit ballots, and Colom's legal counsel answered that the demands "have no basis in Mississippi law" and told counties not to segregate accepted affidavit ballots from other paper ballots. On Friday the NAACP sent its own letter urging election commissions to "strictly adhere to state law during the post-election ballot counting and certification process." Mississippi has no automatic recount law, and a recount can only happen if a court orders one in response to a lawsuit against a county or its election commission, so any fight would play out county by county. Nov. 10 is the deadline for affidavit voters who lacked photo ID to present it, and the last day for mail ballots to arrive and be counted.

items.title: What to Stream: U2, ‘Misty Green,’ ‘The Chosen’ and Randy Travis – WTOP News
items.excerpt: By The Associated Press November 9, 2026 | 12:01 AM ... U2’s new album and Chris Rock’s latest film are some of the new television, films, music and games headed to a device near you. Also among the streaming offerings worth your time this week, as selected by The Associated Press’ entertainment journalists: a “Proud Family” Christmas special, a new season of “The Chosen” and an album of unreleased Randy Travis music. ## New movies to stream from Nov. 9–15 — It’s been 11 years since Chris Rock directed a feature. In “Misty Green” (Nov. 9 on Netflix), Rock returns as writer and director of a Hollywood character study. Rosalind Eleazar (“Slow Horses”), in a breakthrough performance, stars as a talented but self-sabotaging Los Angeles actor whose once bright future in the industry is fading. In his review, AP’s Mark Kennedy called it “one of Rock’s best projects, boosted by the ferocious abilities of Rosalind Eleazar as Misty.” — “Being Heumann” (Nov. 13 on Apple TV), Siân Heder’s follow-up to the best picture-winning family drama “CODA,” is about disability rights pioneer Judy Heumann and the 1977 San Francisco sit-in that helped lead to making federal spaces accessible. Ruth Madeley stars as Heumann in a film richly detailed with the day-to-day challenges of a 28-day demonstration by people with disabilities. Co-starring Mark Ruffalo. — “Avedon” (Nov. 11 on Netflix) chronicles the life and work of photographer Richard Avedon. Directed by Ron Howard, the documentary draws on extensive access to Avedon’s personal archives to explore how his eye for fashion, people and more shaped the imagery of the 20th century. — AP Film Writer Jake Coyle ## New music to stream from Nov. 9–15 — U2 is back. Did you miss them? “Carnaval De Luz” is the Irish rock band’s first full-length release since 2017’s “Songs of Experience.” “Carnaval De Luz” — which translates from Spanish and Portuguese to “Carnival of Light” — is produced by Jacknife Lee, who has been working with U2 since 2004’s “How to Dismantle an Atomic Bomb.” There’s a lot to be excited about in that last sentence alone, and then there’s this: The last track on the album is “Torn,” a duet with Dolly Parton that turned out to be her last recorded vocal performance. — In July 2013, country star Randy Travis was hospitalized with viral cardiomyopathy, a virus that attacks the heart, and later suffered a stroke. The Country Music Hall of Famer had to relearn how to walk, spell and read in the years that followed. A condition called aphasia limits his ability to speak — it’s why it felt like a miracle when he released a new acoustic ballad in 2024, “Where That Came From,” utilizing artificial intelligence to get his voice back. Now, on Friday, he’ll release “Same Old Way,” his first album of original music in over 18 years featuring previously unreleased tracks. No AI here, but all Travis. — The hyperpop hero 2hollis returns with “Pirouette” on Friday, a post-internet, post-Skrillex discordant release — 16 tracks of EDM-indebted future-seeking dance music. He’s a rapper (“Warhorse”) except when he’s not (“Sex”) and something else entirely (“Hurt.”) This one’s for his dedicated fans and those unafraid to join him. — AP Music Writer Maria Sherman ## New series to stream from Nov. 9–15 — Chris Harrison is back to matchmaking with Fox Nation’s first original dating show called “Chris Harrison’s The Vow.” It debuts Wednesday with two episodes, then goes weekly. Jace Cates, 30, courts 10 women looking to get married. Harrison hosted “The Bachelor” franchise for nearly two decades before exiting in 2021 after racial comments about a contestant. The show centers on faith and shared values, and the women are urged to leave if the match isn’t working. Former “Bachelor” Sean Lowe and his wife, Catherine, drop in with advice. — Hulu’s “Rivals” returns Wednesday for the second half of Season 2 with three episodes dropping at once, and the last three arriving weekly. The Emmy- and BAFTA-winning series is adapted from the novel “Rivals” by Jilly Cooper. It’s about two men (played by David Tennant and Aidan Turner) feuding over a British TV franchise. — Peacock releases all six episodes of the limited series “The Good Daughter” on Thursday. It’s based on Karin Slaughter’s 2017 novel. Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy play Samantha and Charlotte Quinn, sisters who are still grappling with a brutal crime that struck their family decades earlier. Slaughter wrote all the episodes. Brendan Gleeson co-stars. — Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan star in and executive-produce the eight-episode series “12 12 12,” debuting Friday. Mackie plays a disgraced FBI agent on the trail of Dornan’s character, a thief who robs a Zurich bank vault. The story shifts between three timelines: 12 months of planning, 12 hours of execution and 12 days on the run. — “The Proud Family” has a Christmas special called “A Proud Family Wizmas,” a stop-motion musical coming to Disney+ on Saturday. Penny Proud’s rant about the commercialization of Christmas causes Santa to quit on Christmas Eve, so she reluctantly steps into his suit to deliver presents. — The first three episodes of Prime Video’s “The Chosen” Season 6 drop Sunday. Jonathan Roumie returns as Jesus in a season about his last day, building to the crucifixion. The finale is headed to theaters next spring. — AP Writer Alicia Rancilio

items.title: Anthony Ippolito & AnnaSophia Robb Open Up About Their Characters In 'I Play Rocky' At Premiere - uInterview
items.excerpt: By Alexis Diggs November 9, 2026, 1:20 am Amazon MGM Studios’ *I Play Rocky* made its West Coast premiere at the iconic TCL Chinese Theatre as part of the AFI Fest. The event kicked off with a bustling red carpet, where director **Peter Farelly**, along with **Anthony Ippolito**, **AnnaSophia Robb**, **Stephan James** and **Kiki Seto**, posed for photos and gave red carpet interviews. The atmosphere stayed high-energy and celebratory throughout the night, with enthusiastic applause at key moments and a raucous standing ovation to top it off. The film is an electrifying true story about an unknown actor with an unshakable belief that he wasn’t just meant to write Rocky—he was meant to be Rocky. After being told “no” at every turn, **Sylvester Stallone** (Ippolito) bets everything on himself and holds the line to play the lead against seemingly impossible odds. The result is the ultimate underdog story behind the underdog movie. Farrelly said Stallone shared many key details about the film, including that he listened to music while writing the Rocky script. “Stallone actually gave us so many important small details,” says Farrelly. “One of the many was the music he listened to while he wrote the *Rocky* script; he has said he wrote it in three and a half days, and he listened to a lot of music. ... Robb plays Sasha Czack, Stallone’s girlfriend and first wife. Sasha typed up the script Stallone wrote by hand and took photos on set once production began. ... *I Play Rocky *is now in select theaters and will be released nationwide on Nov. 20.
